latin.meaning: slippery, smooth; treacherous, deceitful; morally slippery, uncertain
latin.etymology: From PIE *sleubʰ- (to slide, slip), related to lābor (to slip, glide). The same root gives English 'lubricate' and 'sleeve'.
latin.literary_context: Ovid uses lūbricus in the Metamorphoses to describe the snake into which Cadmus transforms, emphasizing its smooth, gliding motion. Tacitus employs it metaphorically in the Annals to characterize the treacherous nature of court politics under Tiberius.
latin.usage_example: Lūbrica serpentis corpora in herbā iacent. — The slippery bodies of snakes lie in the grass.
latin.did_you_know: The Romans applied lūbricus both to physical slipperiness and to moral unreliability, creating a metaphor still alive in English when we speak of 'slippery characters' or 'slippery slopes' in ethics and politics.

greek.meaning: violent arrogance, insolent pride, outrage against the gods or mortals
greek.forms: nom. ὕβρις, gen. ὕβρεως, dat. ὕβρει, acc. ὕβριν; plural ὕβρεις
greek.etymology: From Proto-Indo-European *ud-gʷr-i-, literally 'over-heavy' or 'overgrown.' Related to the verb ὑβρίζω 'to commit hubris, to act with insolent violence.'
greek.literary_context: Aeschylus uses ὕβρις throughout the Oresteia as the root cause of the house of Atreus's downfall, particularly in Agamemnon when the chorus warns that hybris breeds ate (ruin). Herodotus presents the Persian king Xerxes as the paradigm of hybris in his Histories, attributing the Persian defeat at Salamis to his overweening pride.
greek.usage_example: ὕβρις γὰρ ἐξανθοῦσα καρπὸν ἔτισεν ἄτης. — For hybris, when it blooms, bears a harvest of ruin. (Aeschylus, Persians 821-822)
greek.did_you_know: The concept of hybris was not merely psychological but religious: Greeks believed that excessive pride provoked divine retribution (nemesis), making it a cardinal transgression in both tragedy and historiography.

french.forms: singular: foudre; plural: foudres. Also used in phrase 'coup de foudre' (love at first sight, literally 'lightning strike').
french.etymology: From Latin fulgur (lightning, flash), through the accusative form. Related to fulgere (to shine, flash). The shift from neuter Latin to feminine French follows standard Romance evolution.
french.literary_context: Racine employs 'foudre' in Phèdre when the tormented queen invokes Jupiter's thunderbolt to strike her down for her forbidden passion: 'Que ne suis-je assise à l'ombre des forêts! / Quand pourrai-je, au travers d'une noble poussière, / Suivre de l'œil un char fuyant dans la carrière?' The image recurs when she cries for divine punishment.
french.usage_example: Il tomba foudroyé comme par la foudre divine. — He fell struck down as if by divine lightning.
french.did_you_know: In classical French theater, 'foudre' carried both literal meteorological meaning and metaphorical weight as divine judgment. The phrase 'les foudres de l'Église' (the thunderbolts of the Church) referred to excommunication and papal censure.

german.meaning: overman, superman; higher human type transcending conventional morality
german.forms: singular: der Übermensch, des Übermenschen, dem Übermenschen, den Übermenschen; plural: die Übermenschen
german.etymology: From über (over, beyond) + Mensch (human being). While the components existed earlier, Nietzsche gave the term philosophical weight in Thus Spoke Zarathustra (1883-1885), drawing on Goethe's use in Faust.
german.literary_context: Nietzsche's Also sprach Zarathustra introduces the Übermensch as humanity's goal: one who creates values rather than inheriting them, who affirms life fully without recourse to otherworldly consolations. Goethe's Faust uses the term more loosely for exceptional human capacity.
german.usage_example: Der Mensch ist etwas, das überwunden werden soll. Was habt ihr getan, ihn zu überwinden? Alle Wesen bisher schufen etwas über sich hinaus: und ihr wollt die Ebbe dieser großen Flut sein? — Man is something that shall be overcome. What have you done to overcome him? All beings so far created something beyond themselves: and you want to be the ebb of this great flood?
german.did_you_know: The concept was grotesquely distorted by Nazi ideology, though Nietzsche despised antisemitism and nationalism. His sister Elisabeth, who controlled his literary estate, selectively edited his writings to suit völkisch interpretations he would have rejected.

oldenglish.forms: nom. sāwol, acc. sāwle, gen. sāwle, dat. sāwle; plural sāwla/sāwle
oldenglish.etymology: From Proto-Germanic *saiwulō (soul, life force), cognate with Old Saxon sēola, Old High German sēula, Gothic saiwala. Possibly from PIE *sai-wo- (from the sea, vivifying moisture), linking the concept of soul with vital fluids.
oldenglish.literary_context: This word appears prominently in The Dream of the Rood, where the Cross speaks of Christ's sāwol departing: the poet describes the moment of death as the separation of the noble soul from the body, a central theme in Anglo-Saxon Christian poetry exploring mortality and redemption.
oldenglish.usage_example: Sāwol sceal of līce. — The soul must depart from the body.
oldenglish.did_you_know: The feminine gender of sāwol in Old English contrasts with the masculine gāst (spirit), allowing Anglo-Saxon poets to explore nuanced theological distinctions between the immortal soul and the divine spirit that were central to early medieval Christianity.
